purpose: This patch is used to relieve pain in a specific area of your skin, especially pain caused by nerve damage after shingles (a condition called postherpetic neuralgia). It can also be used for other types of localized nerve or muscle pain. It helps reduce pain right where you place it without affecting the rest of your body much.
how_it_works: Lidocaine works by temporarily blocking the pain signals in the nerves under your skin. Think of it like putting a 'mute button' on the nerves in that area so they can't send pain messages to your brain. The medicine stays mostly in the skin and does not get absorbed into your bloodstream in large amounts, which makes it pretty safe to use.
common_side_effects: The most common side effects are right where you place the patch — you might notice mild redness, itching, swelling, or a slight burning or bruising feeling on your skin. These usually go away on their own and are generally mild. Rarely, some people may have a more serious skin rash or allergic reaction.
warnings: Do not use this patch on broken, irritated, or infected skin. Keep it away from your eyes, mouth, and open wounds. Do not wear more patches than prescribed or leave them on longer than directed, as too much lidocaine absorbed into the blood can cause dizziness, irregular heartbeat, or seizures. Tell your doctor if you take other medications, especially heart rhythm medicines. Store used patches safely away from children and pets, as they still contain medicine.
typical_dosing: The usual dose is to apply up to 3 patches to the painful area at one time. You wear the patch for 12 hours, then take it off for 12 hours — this is sometimes called a '12 hours on, 12 hours off' schedule. Cut the patch to size if needed to fit the area. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions for your situation.
